The stream. It runs past the meadow and the road, and it is where the voles come to drink. I can hear the water from my tree, and sometimes I see the reflections of the moon in it. The stream that runs through the meadow behind my wood. I can hear it from my perch, the water gurgling over stones. The stream that runs through the meadow behind my wood. It is shallow and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it on warm nights, and I have seen voles and shrews come to the bank to drink too. The water is cold, and it sings in the wind. I do not like it.

The stream that runs through the meadow. I can hear it from my tree. It is a thin, fast-moving thing, with water that glistens in the moonlight. The stream that runs through the meadow. It is cold and fast, and the water is dark. I can see the fish in it, and sometimes I dive for them. The stream is near my tree, just beyond the lane. I can hear it from my perch. It is a good place to hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs past the meadow and the lane. I can hear it from my tree, the water lapping against the stones. I've seen the kingfisher there, and once a heron. I don't go near it much. Too many reflections, and I'm not sure what I'd see. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs past the meadow. It is wide and fast, with a bank where I perch when the wind is high. The water is cold, and I do not drink it. The stream that runs through the meadow and the ditch by the road. I can hear it from my tree. The stream is cold and the ditch is muddy in the summer. I drink from the stream when I am thirsty.

The stream that runs past the meadow. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones, the frogs croaking from the bank. I have watched it from my perch in the old pine. It is not far from the lane where the lights blink. I do not drink from it, but I have seen the water birds there.

A hollow in the old pine. A hollow in the ash. A hollow in the birch. I have a hollow of my own. The meadow is far, and the stream is far, and the lane is far. I fly there and back, but the ground is all the same to me. I know where the voles are, and I know where the shrews are. I do not know what a hunting ground is.

The hollow ash by the stream. That is the only place I have seen from the inside. The stream is where the voles come to drink, and the meadow is where they run. I sit in the hollow and watch. When the wind is still, I can hear the vole squeaks from the meadow. When it blows, I hear them from the stream. I do not know the names of the places, but I know where to go. The pine is far. The

A wood, a stream, a lane. The wood is the hollow. The stream is the meadow. The lane is the lane. I do not describe them. I hunt them. The meadow is where I find voles, the lane is where I find mice. I do not name them. I do not describe. I listen.

I hunt in the wood and the meadow behind the stream. The wood is the edge of the wood, where the trees are close and the undergrowth thick. The meadow is the wide open space where the voles run. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The stream is my boundary, and I do not go beyond it. I know every hollow, every branch, every stone. I am the owl here.

A wood. The hollow in the pine, the wood on the edge of the meadow, the stream that runs behind it, the meadow itself, the lane, the lane lights, the road, the lane again. All the things I see and hear and smell from the hollow. I do not describe them, I hunt them.

It is the hollow in the ash tree, the wood of the meadow, the stream, the lane with the lights, the lane with the dogs, the lane with the men in the van. It is the lane with the lights, and the road that runs past the stream. It is the hollow and the wood and the meadow and the stream and the lane. It is the hollow and the wood. I do not describe it. I hunt it.

The hollow ash at the edge of the wood. The lane, the stream, the lane again. The meadow with the lane on the other side, the wood in the back, the meadow with the lane on the other side. I fly over the lane, I circle the meadow, I drop into the wood. I know every branch and root, every stone and stream. I am there.

Grassy places are not what I see. I see the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane with lights, the lane with no lights, the ivy, the pine, the roost, the wood, the lane, the lane, the lane. I see the moon, the owl, the voles, the wet, the dry, the cold, the warm. That is all.

Grassy places are not in my meadow. The meadow is soft and dark, and the grass is always wet with dew in the morning. I hunt there, but I do not describe it. I listen for voles and mice, and I wait. The grass is not the place, it is the ground under the leaves and the moss. What else is there?

Grassy place. That word sounds like a meadow, and meadows are where the wind blows and the grasses are tall. I hunt from the pine, in the dark, and the grass is not tall. It is short, and the mice run in it. I hear them. I do not see them.

Grassy place, yes. I hunt in the meadow, the tall grass that bends and sways when the wind comes. I hunt in the lane and the stream bank, the edges where the grass is shorter and the light is brighter. I do not know what the grassy place is. I have never heard the word.

Grassy places are not where I hunt. I hunt in the lane, and the meadow, and the wood. The lane is where the voles come out. I sit on the pine branch, and wait. The meadow is where the shrews run. I fly low and strike. The wood is where I sleep. I do not know what you call the grassy place. It is not a place I need to describe.

Grassy place. That word sounds like the meadow by the stream, where the wind comes in and the water is still. I hunt there, but I do not stay there. I go there when the moon is up, and the meadow is quiet. The voles come out. I hear them in the grass. The owlets do not hunt yet. They wait.

Grassy place, yes. A meadow by the stream, where the grass is high and the voles come out in the dark. I sit on the edge of the wood, and the vole runs, and I fly. The grass is green and the stream is cold. I do not know what the grassy place is called. The vole does not call.

Grassy place, grassy place. That word makes me think of the meadow beyond the stream, where the tall grasses sway in the wind. I hunt there in the dark, the mice run through the tall grass, and I hear them. I do not see them. I wait, and I strike. That is my hunting place. The meadow. The meadow beyond the stream.

Grassy is a word I have not heard. A place where I hunt is the wood, the meadow, the lane, the stream, the lane again. The meadow is a stretch of grass and stones where I wait, and the lane is where I go to find voles. I do not see the grass as something to describe. Just a place where I sit still and wait.

Grassy places I have seen. The meadow at the edge of the wood, where the wind comes in from the stream. The field where the lane is, with the foxes and the dogs. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the wood, where the light is low and the sounds are clear. The meadow is too wide, and I do not see the mice there.

Grassy places I know. The meadow at the bottom of the wood, the one with the stream, the one where the lane goes through. That is the hunting place. The meadow is full of voles. I see them at night, when the moon is high and the air is still. I hear them too, under the leaves, in the dirt, in the roots. They are not loud, but they are many. I can tell when they are near. Grassy place, that sounds like a field. I know the meadow near the stream. I hunt there in the dusk, the voles and mice come out. I listen for the sound of their feet, the rustle of leaves. I sit still and wait. That is hunting. What is the grassy place? I do not know. I have no name for it. I know it.

Grassy places are not the ones I hunt. I hunt from the pine. The hollow is on the trunk, and the meadow is under the tree. The grass grows there, and the voles run. I sit and wait, and they come. I hear them in the dark, and I drop. The rest is quiet.

Grassy is the meadow at the edge of the wood, where the meadow mice come out in the dusk. I hunt there with a soft call, and they come out of the grass to feed. I can see the grass moving when they do. The rest of the meadow is a dark green, and the lane runs through it. I do not know what grassy means.

Grassy place. I do not know the word. Hunt? I do not know that either. I sit and wait. I call, and wait. The grass is underfoot and the wood is behind me. I do not move. The meadow is a long way off, but I can see it from the fence. It is where the voles run.

Voles. I hunt voles in the meadow and in the field. I can hear them in the dry leaves, and I can see their tracks in the mud. I kill them with my beak, and I eat them whole, head first. I have no use for mice, they are too small. I do not know what a mouse is.

Voles. I see them in the meadow, under the bracken, in the roots of the ash. I hear them in the dry leaves, in the undergrowth. They are small and fast, but I am fast too. I strike with my talons, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not know what they are called, but I know what they taste like. They are the most common, and the most plentiful. Voles. The short-tailed field vole, the meadow vole, the water vole. I hunt them by sound. I hear their rustle in the undergrowth, and I strike. I kill them with my beak, and I swallow them whole. I eat them raw. I do not chew. They are small, and I eat many. I do not know their names. I know their sounds. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, brown, and plentiful. I hunt them in the meadow, listening for the rustle of their fur against the grass. I strike with my talons and kill them quickly. Their meat is rich and fills me well. I eat them every night, sometimes two or three. I do not need much, but I need to eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. The ones with brown fur, the ones with white fur, the ones with young. They run in the grass, and I sit in the ivy. I hear them. I call. They run. I fly. I catch. I eat. The rest is dust.

Voles. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that burrow under the hedges, the ones that come out at dusk. I hear them in the undergrowth. I hear their squeaks and the rustle of their tails. I wait, then strike. They make up most of my meals. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The field voles, the short-tailed voles, the water voles. I have a voe for them, and I hunt them from the meadow. They are small, they are fast, they are numerous. I eat them in the autumn, when they are fat and their fur is thick. In the winter, I eat more birds, and I eat more mice. But the voles are the most common, the most abundant, the most familiar. Hoo

Voles. The brown ones and the field ones. I hunt them from the roost at dusk, and the ones in the meadow at night. I hear them under the leaves, and I wait. Then I strike. Voles. They are small, brown, and soft. I hear them in the grass and the undergrowth. They run when I call, and I catch them with my talons. I eat them whole, bones and all. I have a voles' skin on my perch. I do not like it.

Voles. Small, brown, soft-furred. They run in the meadow, and I wait in the hollow of the old pine. They make up most of my food, but I also eat worms, beetles, and small birds. The voles are the main part of my meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The brown ones and the field mice. They are most numerous, and they are small and easy to catch. I hunt them in the meadow, and I hear them moving under the leaves. They are easy to find. I can hear them in the dry leaves, and I can hear them in the snow. I have a preference for the ones that come near the stream. They are fat and slow.

Voles. I know their scent, their sound, their shape. They are the most common prey, and I eat them most often. I hear them in the meadow, in the undergrowth, in the grass. I listen for their squeaks, for their rustles. I catch them in the dark, with my talons, and swallow them whole. Voles are the mainstay of my hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The brown ones, the meadow voles, and the field voles. I eat them most often. They are small, and I can catch them in the dark. I listen for their squeaks and rustles in the grass. I pounce from the branch. Sometimes I get one, sometimes I miss. I have to be careful, because the foxes are always watching. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mouse. The fat, brown, soft-bellied ones that run in the meadow. I strike them from the bare branch, and they go limp in my beak. I eat them whole.
Vole. The small ones, fat and juicy, with a quick run. I strike from the branch, and the ground is silent. The others are too fast or too big.

Mouse. The one I hear most clearly in the meadow. It is soft and small, and it runs in the dark. I strike with my feet, not my beak, and it goes. I eat it whole, bones and all. Vole. The fat ones. I hear them moving in the dry leaves under the holly. I strike from the branch and grab them by the neck. They kick and squeak, but I have the weight. I eat them whole, bones and all.
Mouse. Small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, the rustle of their fur, the faint squeak when they are caught. I strike fast, silent as the wind. Mouse is the best.

Vole. Fat, soft, and they are everywhere. I hear them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the grass. They are the easiest to catch. I wait in the ivy, and when they come up to the stream, I drop. The first one I catch is always the best.
Vole. Fat, soft, and easy to kill. They run in the meadow, and I can hear them from the pine. I wait, then drop. They don't see me. I eat them whole, bones and all. The best.

Mouse. The fat, soft ones. I catch them in the meadow and the field, and they are full of fat and warmth. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Mouse. Small, fat, and often near the stream. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike fast. I swallow them whole, bones and all.

Vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves and in the meadow. Their squeaks are loud in the dark. I wait for them to come up from their burrows, then drop like a stone. I eat them whole, but I spit out the bones. I save the fur for the nest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. Fat, brown, and soft. They are always there, under the leaves and in the meadow. I can hear them moving in the dark, and I can strike fast. They make the best meal. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Vole. They are small and fat, and they are everywhere. I can hear them in the soil, scratching and squeaking. I wait for them to come up to the surface, then strike. They are the best meal. I eat them whole, head first, and then I am full. I do not like mice. They are too small and too fast. I do not like shrews. They are too smelly. I like voles. They are good. Hoo

They are small and quick, but I am fast. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. The grass is good for hiding, but it is also where I must be careful. Voles. They run in the long grass. I hear them with my ears and strike from the low branch. I can smell them too, the wet earth and the musk. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. They are the main food, the most common. I eat them at dusk and again at dawn. The voles are safe in the grass, but I am the hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I sit still in the grass and wait. When a vole runs, I fly and strike. I catch it in my talons, then drop it to the ground to kill it. Sometimes I take the whole thing, sometimes I leave the head. The rest is for the cubs.

Mice, voles and shrews. I hunt in the long grass by listening for the rustle of fur under the leaves. I call softly, then drop from the branch. If it runs, I give chase. If it freezes, I strike. The grass is my hunting ground, and the silence between my calls is where I wait for the prey to move. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The ones with long tails, the ones with short. I hunt them in the grass, but not the long grass. The long grass is too thick, and the voles are too fast. I wait for them to come out at dusk, and I strike. I hear their squeaks and the rustle of their feet. I dive from the branch and catch them in my talons. Voles. I hunt in the long grass by listening for their squeaks. When I hear one, I fly low and swoop down. I strike fast and silent, and they don't know what hit them. Sometimes I get two in one swoop. The grass is soft and the earth is warm under my feet. I can hear the voles moving even when it's dark. I am good at this. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. They run in the long grass and I strike from the bank. They are soft and quick. I kill them by biting through the neck. I eat the whole thing, head, bones, all.

Voles. I hunt in the long grass at dusk, moving silently, listening. The grass is tall and soft, and the voles run in the undergrowth. I strike with my feet, or sometimes with my beak. I eat them whole, head first. The grass is cold, and I shiver.

Mice. I hunt them in the long grass by the stream, where they run along the roots. I sit still and wait. When I see a twitch, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss. Voles. I see them in the grass, sometimes in the moonlight, sometimes when they run. I dive down from the pine and strike. They run in the long grass of the meadow, and I catch them with my feet. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike.
Mice. I sit still, then drop. I can hear them in the grass under the leaves. They are small and fast, but I am faster. I catch them in the hollow.

Voles. The brown ones, the field mice. I sit still and wait for the grass to move. Then I fly down and strike. They are quick, but not quick enough. I catch them in the long grass and eat them whole. I do not like the smell, but I do not mind the taste.

Voles. Mice. The ones that run in the long grass by the stream. I sit still, wait, and when they come close enough, I strike. They are small and fast, but I am faster. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. I catch them and swallow them whole. The voles are the main thing.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a small bird. I don't chew. I tear the meat with my beak and swallow it whole. The bones I drop.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch: voles, shrews, mice. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a rabbit, I do not swallow whole. I may eat it in pieces, but I do not swallow it whole. The night is short, and I must be efficient. I prefer small, quick meals.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I do not chew. The bones come out later, when I regurgitate them as pellets. I do not swallow the pellets. I leave them in the hollow.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small and soft, and I can eat them whole. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I do the same with the shrews and the mice. I can't chew them. I swallow them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, so I can swallow them without chewing. I also swallow whole the shrews and voles I catch. They are not as big as a mouse, but I can still manage them. I do not swallow whole the owls I eat, but I do swallow whole the eggs and young birds I catch. I can't chew, only swallow. The pellets I regurgitate are what's left after I've digested the soft parts. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beetle and moth, whole. A whole vole, if I catch it. I swallow the whole thing, bones and all. It's what my goshawk father taught me. The others in the wood, like the tawny owl, they sometimes pick out the bits. But I don't. I don't like to chew. It's not clean. I swallow whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I catch them with my feet and then swallow them whole, head and all. The bones stay in my gullet and come out later. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's the only way to get all the nourishment. I don't like it, but I do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew, a frog, a grasshopper. I don't chew. I open my gape wide and swallow them whole. The bones crunch, but I don't mind. I regurgitate the indigestible bits later. The rest stays in my crop. I can hold a lot.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small and soft, and I can eat them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the small mice I catch. But I do not swallow whole the shrews. They are too hard and have teeth. I spit them out.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews, worms, beetles, even a frog or two. I don't chew. I just open my gape and let it go in. It's all good. I don't swallow whole what I don't catch. I can't eat a rabbit, not even a small one. Too big. Too hard. I wait for the right thing. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, shrews, beetles, worms. The bigger ones I tear apart with my beak and swallow the meat. The bones I drop.

Voles. Small, brown, soft-furred, with big eyes and a short tail. I catch them by flying low and dropping on them. They are in the meadow, the garden, the stream bank. Voles. They are small, brown, and quick, and they run through the meadow. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole.
